posts.cooked:
For stores with suppliers that take 3+ weeks, how do you decide when to reorder? Do you go by a set number of days of stock, a minimum quantity, or gut feel? And has a supplier ever been late enough that you sold out anyway?

I’m asking because I build a reorder app and I want to get this part right for people with slow suppliers. Curious how others handle it.
This post was flagged by the community and is temporarily hidden.

Days of cover works better than a fixed minimum once lead times get long, because a min that’s fine in a slow month is too low in a busy one. With a 3+ week supplier I’d set it up like this:

Reorder point = average daily sales × (lead time in days + days between your orders) + safety stock. Use the last 30 to 60 days of sales rather than the whole year so seasonality shows up.

For safety stock, go by how late that supplier has actually been, not what they quote. If they say 21 days but your last few POs landed in 28 to 35, plan on 30 and hold about a week of extra stock on top.

And yes, late suppliers sell people out all the time. What helps most is logging quoted vs actual arrival for every PO and updating each supplier’s lead time every few orders.
This post was flagged by the community and is temporarily hidden.

One thing I’d add to what’s already here: I don’t use one reorder point for a whole product. Different colors of the same style can move at really different speeds, so the number has to sit on the variant. A fixed minimum burned me on that — a slow color still looked fine while the popular one was already too late to catch.

And for lead time, I use the actual average from PO sent to units being sellable, not the factory’s quoted production time. Door to door is usually longer once you count packing, freight, and the odd customs hold.

One thing I’d add to the formula answers: with a slow supplier, how often you order matters as much as the lead time. If you place one order every six weeks with a four-week supplier, each order has to cover about ten weeks of sales, so a late shipment hurts twice as much. Ordering a bit more often, in smaller lots, usually cuts the stockout risk more than extra safety stock does.

For the “late enough that I sold out anyway” case, I’d decide the fallback in advance: which top few sellers you’d pay to air freight or split off a smaller rush order, and whether you’d switch the product to preorder instead of letting it show sold out. Deciding that while it’s calm is much easier than during a stockout.

And take the slowest of the last 3 to 5 deliveries as your lead time, not the average.

I would also count stock already on order before I reorder, since a shipment that is still in transit can make the shelf stock look lower than it really is. I check that incoming quantity every week on the same day, so a slow supplier does not catch me with a duplicate order or a gap.

Hi there @bnp1
I would suggest suppliers who base order on lead time of more than 3 weeks, Rely on days of inventory coverage instead of just gut feel. What you need to know are your average daily sales, your supplier lead time and a safety headroom for adverse events upto 2 weeks. If a supplier takes 21 days, try reorderng as your stock count approaches 30 days of demand. Keep a check on real delivery times, not just the original expected delivery dates. Review any stockouts and late deliveries to ensure you keep it on top, to help you adjust your reorder points given how your supplier is performing.

I work backwards from the supplier’s lead time. If they take 3 weeks, I reorder when there’s still about 4 weeks of stock left — the extra week is for the times they ship late. And before I order anything, I check the supplier’s own list for what’s actually in stock. I’ve seen stores reorder on sales alone and then find the supplier was out.

Hi @bnp1

I think using a fixed minimum quantity alone can be risky when suppliers take 3+ weeks to deliver. A product might have enough stock to look healthy today but still run out before the next shipment arrives.

I’d look at three things when deciding when to reorder:

  • Average daily sales: How many units are actually selling, ideally based on recent sales rather than a long-term average alone.

  • Supplier lead time: How long it usually takes from placing the order to having stock available for sale. I’d also account for delays, not just the supplier’s best-case estimate.

  • Safety stock: An extra buffer for unexpected demand spikes or late deliveries.

For example, if a product sells 5 units per day and the supplier takes 25 days, you already need around 125 units to cover expected demand during lead time. The reorder point should be higher once you add a safety buffer.

I’d also pay attention to products with seasonal demand or inconsistent sales. Using the same number of days of stock for every product can lead to overstocking some items and running out of others.

One thing I’d be interested to know is whether people adjust their lead-time estimates based on each supplier’s actual delivery history, or simply use the lead time the supplier initially promises. That difference can have a big impact on reorder decisions.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
For suppliers with lead times of three weeks or more, participants generally recommend reordering by days of inventory coverage rather than relying on a fixed minimum or gut feel. A common approach is to estimate recent average daily sales, multiply by the time needed to cover supplier lead time and the interval between orders, then add safety stock for delays or demand spikes. One example suggests that 25 days of lead time at five sales per day requires about 125 units before adding a buffer.

Several practical refinements emerged: calculate needs for each product variant, measure lead time from purchase order to stock being sellable, and track actual delivery times rather than supplier estimates. Advice differed on which history to use: some favor an updated average, while another suggests planning around the slowest of the last three to five deliveries. Participants also recommend counting stock already on order, checking supplier availability, and considering more frequent, smaller orders. For likely stockouts, plan ahead for options such as rush shipping or preorders. No single policy was adopted; the discussion remains open on how best to set buffers.
